title: The Big Ben London
description: A practical London repertoire covering central plans and concrete answers to early challenges.
intro: Build a dependable White repertoire from 1.d4, with the London bishop developed before e3 whenever the position allows it. These ninety lines connect familiar development with the specific pawn breaks and tactical replies each defence demands. We aim for playable middlegames while learning when a quiet setup should give way to active central play. Study the plans first, then use the move sequences to recognise the critical decisions at the board.

chapters.title: Early ...Bd6: keep the central grip
chapters.intro: An early bishop challenge on d6 changes the familiar London structure. Sometimes we allow the exchange and use doubled f-pawns to control e5; sometimes we exchange on d6 and support a central knight with f4. Our light-squared bishop and central rooks need useful squares before an attack can develop. The practical decision is where to shelter the king while Black prepares counterplay with the c-pawn.

chapters.title: Classical centre: build around e5
chapters.intro: Black supports the classical d5 centre with e6, giving us time to organise our pieces around e5. We learn when to preserve the London bishop, when a central exchange improves our structure, and how the queen can join a kingside attack. The attacking lines require calculation, especially before a sacrifice. Our guiding question is whether Black can free the position with ...e5 before we establish our pieces.

chapters.title: Active bishops: gain space with tempo
chapters.intro: An active black bishop and an early ...c5 challenge require us to read the precise central structure. A queen on b3 can pressure b7, while knight manoeuvres and kingside pawns can pursue an exposed bishop. We also study the tactical danger of a queen on d7. The guiding idea is to connect each space-gaining move with a concrete target while keeping the centre protected.

chapters.title: Queen raids: develop with threats
chapters.intro: An early queen attack on b2 asks us to think beyond the usual London formation. We answer with development, central exchanges and threats against the queen or the uncastled king, choosing our knight square according to the move order. Some lines keep material balanced; others invest a pawn in activity. The key skill is recognising when a tempo against the queen makes a central break or a tactical capture possible.

chapters.title: Slav structures: use the queenside
chapters.intro: Black's c6 pawn supports d5 but also defines targets on the queenside. We often use c4 and Qb3 to ask immediate questions, with the possibility of either a tactical bishop incursion or a queenless position with an active a-file. Early queen attacks against b2 require a different response, sometimes involving a pawn sacrifice. Throughout the chapter, central control and precise move order matter more than repeating a fixed setup.

chapters.title: Symmetrical bishops: break the copycat
chapters.intro: When Black brings the light-squared bishop out early, the position can look symmetrical without remaining quiet. We challenge that bishop with Bd3, use e5 when a knight gains time there, and accept doubled d-pawns when they support central expansion. Several lines show why the order of captures matters. Our aim is to turn small differences in tempo, king safety and pawn structure into a clear middlegame plan.

chapters.title: Chigorin: challenge the early knight
chapters.intro: An early knight on c6 gives Black active development but obstructs the c-pawn. If the other knight has already reached f6, Bb5 and Ne5 can create tactical pressure on c6. When Black leaves the g8 knight flexible, our c-pawn often challenges d5 instead. We will distinguish those move orders, then practise turning exchanges into either a structural target or a coordinated attack against the king.

chapters.title: Early challenges: Englund and Tarrasch
chapters.intro: These immediate central challenges require a different response from quiet London development. Against the Englund, we accept the pawn and learn to meet queen checks and pressure on c2 without losing coordination. Against an early c5, we either build a supported queenside pawn chain or open the centre with e4. The recurring lesson is to calculate checks and intermediate attacks before recapturing, then finish development as soon as the forcing sequence ends.

chapters.title: Queen's Indian: meet the fianchetto
chapters.intro: The bishop on b7 makes Black's central pawn breaks especially important. We develop compactly, preserve our active bishops when useful and place the rooks before opening the centre. When Black settles into a restrained formation with d6 and e6, our knights can regroup while the a- and c-pawns create queenside contact. The aim is steady pressure, with enough attention to ...e5 and ...b5 that our extra space remains useful.

chapters.title: King's Indian: build a broad centre
chapters.intro: Against the kingside fianchetto, we use c3 and Nbd2 to prepare a broader centre with e4. Black will challenge that centre with pawn breaks, so the key decisions concern exchanges and the protection of e4. We also study an ambitious bishop sacrifice when Black overextends before castling. Most positions call for coordinated development and central files; an extra pawn still requires careful consolidation against active pieces.

chapters.title: Grünfeld: reinforce the centre
chapters.intro: Black combines a bishop on g7 with a pawn on d5, challenging our central formation from two directions. Sometimes we can capture c5 and defend the extra pawn; in other lines we protect our bishop or start a direct kingside attack. The sharpest examples involve opening the h-file at a material cost. We always connect those attacks with piece development and account for Black’s central counterplay.

chapters.title: Benoni and Dutch: answer flank play
chapters.intro: Flank openings change where our play belongs. The Benoni positions reward control of central squares, restrained queenside counterplay and well-timed pawn advances; against the Dutch, c4 usually gives us a useful challenge to Black's kingside space. Several move orders also contain concrete queen raids or central tactics. We connect each variation to a middlegame plan, while keeping enough flexibility to choose king safety before opening new lines.
